descriptors.descriptor_basis: Interview transcript states respondent is Chair, university research ethics committee.

segments.title: Distinction between research ethics review and system deployment
segments.quote: Only the research on it, not the system itself. That distinction is the whole problem in one sentence.
segments.full_text:
Interview transcript A05 — Chair, university research ethics committee
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] Did any part of this deployment come before your committee?
[Respondent] Only the research on it, not the system itself. That distinction is the whole problem in one sentence. If a doctoral student wants to interview twelve people about the cameras, that comes to me and I will spend forty minutes on the consent form. The decision to install the cameras and point them at a hundred thousand people went through a procurement committee. Nobody thinks this is strange except the people who say it out loud.

codes.rationale: The system deployment bypassed the ethics committee, demonstrating a lack of responsiveness to ethical considerations beyond research.

segments.title: Lack of capacity to review deployments
segments.quote: Not as constituted. We have no authority over the city and no capacity if we did — we're eleven academics and an administrator, meeting six times a year, and we're already behind.
segments.full_text:
Interview transcript A05 — Chair, university research ethics committee
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] Could your committee's remit cover deployments?
[Respondent] Not as constituted. We have no authority over the city and no capacity if we did — we're eleven academics and an administrator, meeting six times a year, and we're already behind. I mention the capacity because people propose expanding ethics review as though review were free.

codes.rationale: The committee lacks the authority and capacity to review deployments, indicating an obdurate inability to adapt to broader ethical concerns.

segments.title: Researcher preparedness for inconvenient findings
segments.quote: What I still almost never see is a plan for what the researcher will do if the finding is inconvenient to the funder.
segments.full_text:
Interview transcript A05 — Chair, university research ethics committee
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] What have you seen change in the studies that do come to you?
[Respondent] More applications now include a data-protection impact assessment, which is progress. What I still almost never see is a plan for what the researcher will do if the finding is inconvenient to the funder. I've started asking for it. Roughly a third of applicants have no answer and about a fifth are visibly irritated that I asked.

codes.rationale: The respondent's questioning of researchers about inconvenient findings demonstrates a move towards epistemic humility and scrutiny of assumptions.

segments.title: Limited public representation on the ethics committee
segments.quote: We have one lay member. One, out of twelve. She is excellent and she is also one person doing the work of a category.
segments.full_text:
Interview transcript A05 — Chair, university research ethics committee
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] Do affected communities have any voice in your process?
[Respondent] We have one lay member. One, out of twelve. She is excellent and she is also one person doing the work of a category. When she can't attend, the public perspective is simply absent from that meeting and we proceed anyway. We should not proceed anyway.

codes.rationale: The limited representation of lay members demonstrates a closed and exclusive approach to public engagement.

summary: The respondent highlights a significant disconnect between research ethics review and the deployment of systems like the Port Calder traffic signal. The committee's limited authority and capacity, coupled with a lack of robust engagement with affected communities, reveals a system struggling to adapt to broader ethical concerns. While there are signs of increased reflexivity, such as the respondent’s questioning of researchers about inconvenient findings, the overall impression is one of a constrained and reactive process, rather than a proactive and inclusive approach to responsible innovation. The respondent’s frustration underscores the need for a more comprehensive and empowered ethics review mechanism that can address the ethical implications of technology deployments beyond the realm of research.
